families.s: HSE reaction-hazard and product-testing technical measures
families.t: runaway reactions, exotherms, decomposition, thermal stability, calorimetry, pressure, scale-up and relief design
f: Reaction-hazard assessment should identify and control exothermic and decomposition hazards.
Runaway reactions occur when heat generation exceeds heat loss.
Batch reactors are common locations for runaway events, but other equipment can also be affected.
Storage vessels, batch distillation and drying operations have experienced severe undesired reactions.
Temperature rise can accelerate reaction rate and pressure generation.
Testing should establish thermal stability, heat release, gas generation and credible runaway conditions.
Scale-up and process changes should use appropriate reaction-hazard data.
Results should inform control, quench, relief, containment and operating procedures.
families.g: Runaway reactions, exotherms, decomposition, thermal stability, calorimetry, pressure, scale-up and relief design guidance is general process-safety evidence and does not prove current controls, condition, inventory, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.s: HSE reliability of utilities for hazardous plant
families.t: electricity, cooling, steam, instrument air, inert gas, backup systems, common cause failure, fail safe and maintenance
f: Reliable utilities are necessary to prevent hazardous equipment failures.
Utility failures can affect a whole site, a local area or part of a single plant.
Loss of power can also cause loss of other dependent utility systems.
Plant should be designed to move to a safe condition after credible utility failures where practicable.
Some processes require local backup because utility loss would otherwise lead to a hazardous event.
Relevant utilities can include electricity, cooling, steam, instrument air, inert gas and communications.
Common-cause and dependent failures should be considered in risk assessment.
Backup systems, changeover arrangements, testing and maintenance should demonstrate required availability.

families.s: HSE pressure-relief and vent-system technical measures
families.t: overpressure, underpressure, fire, maloperation, utility failure, relief valves, bursting discs, discharge and documentation
f: Process plant may experience overpressure or underpressure from fire, maloperation, utility failure, ambient change or reaction.
Inherently safer design should be considered before adding relief systems.
Relief devices should be selected and located to minimise harm to plant and the environment.
A relief device should not be isolated from protected equipment while that equipment is in use.
Relief discharge should be routed to a safe location or treatment system.
The design basis and methodology for relief streams should be documented.
Relief valves require proof checks and seating checks, especially in corrosive service.
Bursting discs respond rapidly but are non-reclosing and require correct design, assembly and maintenance.

families.t: bunds, drip trays, sumps, interceptors, double skins, off-gas treatment, drainage and inspection
f: Secondary containment is a second line of defence against major-hazard releases.
Common forms include bunds, drip trays, sumps, interceptors and double-skinned equipment.
Bunds are used around tanks and drum-storage areas containing flammable or toxic liquids.
Incompatible materials should not share containment that could allow dangerous mixing.
Bund capacity should account for the largest vessel and emergency response additions.
Bund integrity and drainage need inspection and controlled operation.
Drip trays can stop small equipment leaks spreading to other plant or drains.
Drainage and off-gas systems should be designed for the worst credible release and monitored before discharge.

families.t: compatibility, inventories, labelling, zones, oxidisers, flammables, acids, cyanides, drainage and emergency access
f: Segregation is used to minimise foreseeable major-accident risks from stored hazardous materials.
Material properties and chemical compatibility should determine storage groups.
Inventory systems should identify hazardous materials and their locations.
Containers and storage areas require adequate identification and labelling.
Oxidisers, flammables, strong acids, cyanides and reactive materials may require separate zones.
Drainage should not allow incompatible leaks to mix.
Layout should provide ventilation, containment, emergency access and escape routes.
Risk assessment, housekeeping, training and emergency arrangements should support the segregation system.
